speakerposition: topic
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of
the Opposition): Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question arising out of the exchange of letters between himself and the premier of Quebec. Pending the convening of the suggested conference dealing with the urgent matter of protecting investors in corporations, particularly those under federal jurisdiction, what steps is the government taking at this time to apply existing federal authority; and will the Prime Minister say whether any federal investigation is
taking place at the present time into the North American General Insurance Company which operated under a federal charter and federal jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a number of questions were asked about the North American General Insurance Company at the time this company suffered as a result of the failure of its parent, the Prudential Finance Company. I think I answered those questions adequately at that time. If there are any further questions the right hon. gentleman would like to ask I will endeavour to answer them.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I just asked what steps are being taken now. Will the minister say what steps are being taken to assure foreign investors of the security of Canadian companies, other than the distribution of the Prime Minister's statement of February 1 by the Canadian consul general in New York to United States business leaders?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question is of such a general character I am unable to follow it. It may be capable of answer but I think it should be more specific before I undertake to reply.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: Is the minister aware of the fact that the consul general in New York, in order to assure United States businessmen of the security of Canadian shares and stocks, had the Prime Minister's speech distributed to United States business heads? That should be simple enough even for him to understand. When he is answering that question will he also state whether there has been any suggestion that in order to reassure businessmen in the United States regarding Canada's attitude, the Minister without Portfolio be sent on a speaking tour of the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is quite clear that the right hon. gentleman intended to make a statement. He did not ask for my comments.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext:
You haven't got an answer. You did not even know about it.
February 14, 1987

Inquiries of the Ministry

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Further to the exchange between the Prime Minister and the premier of Quebec regarding the federal-provincial conference on financial institutions and securities, I would ask the Prime Minister this question. In addition to the whole question of deposit insurance, what other items does the federal government propose or intend to suggest be placed on the agenda for this conference?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the proposed conference will cover the work of our financial institutions in a general way. We will be communicating later today with all the provinces, and if they have detailed items to suggest for these meetings they can make them known to us. There are discussions going on, I believe, at the present time among the officials of the various governments that will be concerned in working out the agenda for the ministerial conference.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a further supplementary question to the Minister of Finance and ask him how many of the provincial governments have so far officially informed the minister that they intend to introduce legislation making it mandatory for the financial institutions coming within their jurisdiction to bring themselves within the purview of the legislation with which we will be dealing later today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext:
The province of Ontario
through Mr. Rowntree, its minister concerned with these matters, indicated in the Ontario legislature that it would require all Ontario companies to be covered by federal deposit insurance. The attorney general of British Columbia, Mr. Bonner, made a statement to the effect-I have not had any confirmation as yet-that this is the intention of his government. I have communicated with all the other provinces and drawn to their attention the statement I made on second reading. I have not had replies other than those I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I have supplementary question for the right hon. Prime Minister. In view of the fact that he has acquiesced in the suggestion made by Premier Johnson of Quebec as to the holding of a conference on deposit insurance, would the Prime Minister reconsider his position in
[Mr. Diefenbaker.)

respect of Premier Robarts' call for a conference on our constitution, which would be very appropriate at this time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: In the first place, Mr. Speaker, it is not a conference on deposit insurance. In the second place, it is a conference to deal with a matter for which we have already been preparing with the provinces. Premier Johnson's suggestion is that we^ might have that meeting earlier than had been contemplated. Third, there is no connection whatever between a conference on constitutional matters and a conference on financial matters.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, does not the Prime Minister think that a constitutional question is one that comes within the purview of the provinces, or is it only within the jurisdiction of the federal government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: It is also-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: Order, please. I would think the question as asked is not acceptable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should point out, as it is important, that there is also a difference between the two situations, in that Mr. Johnson asked the federal government to call the conference.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: A further supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Would not the Prime Minister take the initiative in respect of the call of Premier Robarts and have the federal government, now that we are in our centennial year, call a conference on the constitution?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: We have asked for it over and over again.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have already indicated that in our view this is not the moment for a full conference on the amending of our constitution, until all the preparatory work has been completed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. What is constitutionally wrong with a provincial government convening a conference, in the absence of the federal government taking the action it should?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCES ON FINANCIAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL MATTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the provincial governments do that every year.

subtopic: LOUISBOURG FORTRESS-DISMISSAL OF SENIOR EMPLOYEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister of northern development. May I ask him whether he is in a position today to reply to a question I posed some days ago with reference to the charge that one Jeremy Akerman had been laid off from his position as an archeologist at the fortress of Louis-bourg project because of political activity on behalf of the New Democratic Party. The minister will recall that he promised me some days ago that he would investigate the matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arihur Laing (Minister of Indian Affairs and Norihern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: LOUISBOURG FORTRESS-DISMISSAL OF SENIOR EMPLOYEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for drawing this matter once more to my attention. The hon. lady member for Vancouver-Kingsway asked yesterday whether I would give a reply.
Mr. Jeremy Akerman was employed by us under contract as a junior archeologist on the Louisbourg project. It became apparent very quickly thereafter that he was interested in other things, when he made a very heavy attack on the operations of the federal fisheries department. My officers drew this to my attention and said that in light of the fact that this was not affecting his work at Louisbourg they did not intend to discipline him; and I agreed with that entirely.
Some time later he went on television and radio attacking his own senior officer in archeology, and my officers have now advised me that they have not the intention of renewing his contract when it expires; and I agree with that, too.
I am now reliably told, Mr. Speaker, that on February 13 Mr. Akerman accepted a nomination from the New Democratic Party in a riding in the province of Nova Scotia. From this I can only conclude that this young
[Mr. McCleave.)

man is determined to spend all his life digging into the past.

subtopic: LOUISBOURG FORTRESS-DISMISSAL OF SENIOR EMPLOYEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure that if he were to dig sufficiently into the past he would find the minister there. May I ask the minister whether he has confirmed by examining the text of the alleged radio and television programs that such an attack was made by this man upon his superiors; and has the minister himself checked to see whether it is true that he did become a candidate for public office? I would also ask the minister whether it is forbidden for civil servants to accept nomination for public office.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: LOUISBOURG FORTRESS-DISMISSAL OF SENIOR EMPLOYEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am assured by my officers that their decisions in both these affairs had nothing to do with any political activity this man was carrying on at all. The contract expires on March 31, 1967 I think, and I assume he will continue to work for us until then. Their decision not to renew his contract had nothing at all to do with his activity but only with his professional capacity.

that the house go into committee to consider Bill No. C-261, to establish the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation.

On clause 2-Definitions.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION, MAKING OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should not want clause 2 to carry in the hubbub of the resumption of the sitting. Clause 2 is the interpretation clause. Because of the rush to get this bill through, the transcript of evidence of the previous proceedings having been delivered to opposition spokesmen only during the lunch hour, it may be a little difficult to operate. With the evidence given by the minister and other persons with regard to this bill coming to hand so late we shall operate under a handicap. However, we shall do our best to discuss this bill section by section. Should there be some duplication between questions asked in the house during the course of debate and questions asked of the minister in the committee, that duplication I hope will be readily understood.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
On the definitions clause the first point I would raise is the question of the definition of a deposit. There was a good deal of discussion on what should be a deposit receiving or accepting institution. In that connection the transcript is wrong where it classifies this as a deposit excepting institution, and I hope whoever has the responsibility for the transcript will make the necessary correction.
If it is impossible for parliament to define in this clause what a deposit is, then what
Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. hope is there for a definition of a deposit in the by-laws of the corporation? Why must the power to define a deposit, or the ambit of this bill, be assigned to the corporation by parliament, particularly since the corporation will not be directly responsible to parliament and not subject to review by parliament, except that its report will be tabled and I suppose we can discuss it on the estimates of the Minister of Finance?
This once more raises a subject I have discussed on many occasions, namely that delegated powers of this kind must at all times be subject to review by parliament, and not by the present procedure. This is a delegated power and parliament, or a committee thereof, must be in a position to annually assess performance under such delegated powers and the delineation of such powers. So far as this house and the other place are concerned, this is writing a blank cheque in that the government, in proposing this bill, has again refused to face up to its responsibilities.
The minister quite candidly admitted that there was difficulty in determining what is a deposit. Do deposits include certain types of demand bonds? Do they include Canada savings certificates? The government are quite content to say "Well, we will let the corporation determine what is a deposit." I cannot conceive any greater type of abdication of government responsibility. I could continue to speak about the abdication of responsibility in regard to the supervision and control of banks and near banks, but I shall not do that now because I will have a great deal to say about the matter when we are discussing the amendments to the Bank Act.
This, Mr. Chairman, is a stop gap measure. The minister said so before the standing committee. If it had not been for the action of the government of the province of Ontario the other day, this measure would not be under discussion now. Right at the very beginning, from page 4 of the transcript, we know that in the ordinary course of events the government would not have come forward with this bill. Why has the government suddenly got cold feet now? It had an appropriate opportunity to cover this matter of supervision and control when drafting the amendments to the Bank Act. It is as if the government came up to the front door, refused to open it, and then came back and tried to get in through a side door with respect to the control and inspection of near banks.
13012	COMMONS
Canada Deposit Insurance Corp.
I shall have more to say with regard to the provision respecting the consent of the provinces, but on this particular clause I ask the minister why it is that we in this house cannot define what is a deposit, in either in general enough terms to accept evolution in, shall I say, quasi banking practices, or if preferred by the draftsman, by itemizing what is meant by a deposit so that it may be clear cut?
The committee is considering deposit insurance, but it does not even know what is a deposit. It merely knows that the corporation, a group of individuals appointed by the crown, will at some future date determine what shall be a deposit. I would have thought an eminent lawyer like the Minister without Portfolio would have wondered at this. I mean the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, since the other Minister without Portfolio is just an accountant in the terminology of other people. Why would the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George accept such a definition in this key clause? The bill is to be known as the "Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act," yet we cannot tell what is a deposit. Somebody else will have to tell parliament what it is. I would like the minister to interpret and explain just what is meant so far as this particular clause is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION, MAKING OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, one of the principal reasons that no attempt has been made in this parliament to define a deposit is that we are going to make these facilities available to provincial corporations as well as to federal corporations. We do know what constitutes a deposit for the purposes of federal institutions. Indeed, the officers of the government are very well aware of the operations of federal institutions which they inspect. However, we are not in a position at the present time to know exactly the form of all the instruments which are issued by provincial companies, since we do not exercise any supervision over them. We have been urged by the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec to leave some flexibility in the legislation so we do not inadvertently leave out of the ambit of a deposit some instrument that, on examination, we might wish to insure.
When I spoke on second reading of the bill and in the standing committee I gave a general idea of the kind of deposits that would be insured. Of course in the bill itself such deposits are limited to $20,000, so we are not

DEBATES	February 14, 1967
asking for carte blanche. There are limitations in the bill, but generally speaking we would try to include deposits of up to five years maturity.
Another reason that I think it would be undesirable to attempt to define a deposit too precisely in the bill is that we shall endeavour to persuade institutions that come under our policies to make clear, on the face of those deposits that are insured, that they are in fact deposits. This may require a change in nomenclature or description, and for these reasons I believe the government is justified in asking the house to approve the bill with a considerable degree of flexibility in it. After we have had some experience it may be possible for us to describe more precisely in legislation the kind of instruments that hereafter would be insured. At the present stage, since this is the first legislation of its kind ever introduced in the house, I submit that some flexibility is desirable.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION, MAKING OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we in the New Democratic Party have serious objections to the failure of the government to define a deposit. Probably the minister is aware that in the United States under the Federal-Savings and Loan Insurance Corporation and also under the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation a deposit is defined. In the Federal Savings Loan Insurance Corporation accounts are defined as all forms of savings and insured savings including share and investment certificates, while the F.D.I.C. insures demand savings and short-term deposits in commercial and savings banks.
The hon. member for Edmonton West has raised an excellent point with regard to what constitutes a deposit. One of the things which worried so many people in Ontario with regard to the Prudential Finance fiasco was that they thought they had deposits in particular institutions because they held guaranteed savings certificates. If we do not include these in our definition, we will be in very serious trouble because, as the minister well knows, the coverage in this bill does not include finance institutions. Many people making deposits in these institutions may well think that they are covered by this bill when in fact they will not be. One of the disappointments with regard to the Prudential affair was the failure of the government either to set up a royal commission on its own or jointly with the province to determine the reasons for the failure of that company. Such a commission
February 14, 1967	COMMONS
could have made recommendations with regard to such types of institutions which will not be covered by this legislation.
One comment made by the minister which is most welcome is the statement that depositors who will be covered by this legislation should and must know whether they have deposits within the definition contained therein. We welcome this because of the complexity of the definition and the difficulty which most people have in determining whether they have deposits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION, MAKING OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to make one short comment on the statement just made. While it is true that the provision before us does not define a deposit, deposits will be defined by the corporation and due notice will be given to all institutions and to all depositors of the exact description of the deposits which ultimately will be insured.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION, MAKING OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps this point is open to argument. We are going to allow the corporation to define deposits if we pass this bill. By delegating the authority to the corporation we are taking it away from parliament. Why cannot parliament define deposits?
As found on page 8 of the transcript of evidence, in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, the minister said that he had not seen the Ontario legislation but that he understood it would require all Ontario companies to join the federal scheme once it is in effect. I take it that this means all Ontario companies taking deposits. Therefore it would seem to me that Ontario at least must have a definition of deposits.
I claim, that some of the provincial companies actually are under federal jurisdiction with regard to deposit-taking but the government does not exert its authority. However, in respect of the companies which are under federal jurisdiction because of the definition in the Bank Act and because of their charters, surely the minister must know which of their instruments are going to be insured. Therefore, why can they not be defined in the bill by such words as "such other instruments as may be determined by the corporation in consultation with the provinces"? At least parliament would have indicated its authority to that extent.
What we object to is the principle of delegating to a corporation the power to define what the bill actually covers. Our position, which I feel is justified, is that parliament
Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. when it is passing an act should define what it covers. When it is necessary that we know the definition of instruments in respect of federal companies which are going to be insured, why can this not be stated?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION, MAKING OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think
we would advance our legislation very far if we were to say that deposits include what clearly are deposits, such as notice and demand deposits of chartered banks. That would be easy and obviously is covered by the bill. The more difficult cases arise when we get into deposit receipts which could be regarded from one point of view as a security and from another point of view as a deposit. That is where the complications arise. In preparing this legislation it seemed to us that in order to make the bill as useful as possible it would be satisfactory to the house to give the corporation some flexibility. Anything which obviously is a deposit will be insured. The problem is, what is the difference between a deposit and a security? We felt it desirable to study this question at some length, have some discussion with the provinces about the differences in practice, and endeavour to persuade the institutions concerned to make a clear distinction. In that way the public would be given greater security.
I do not think it will advance the cause at all if we say that deposits include notice and demand deposits in the chartered banks. That is obvious. If the committee wishes to amend the bill to the effect that it shall include notice and demand deposits and such other instruments as may be defined by the Governor in Council, I have no objection, but I do not think this will in any way clarify the situation for the general public nor for our discussions with the provinces.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION, MAKING OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the minister would be just a little more precise in respect of one form of deposit. In recent times perhaps the most popular instruments which have been issued by near banks are what are called guaranteed investment certificates. Is it clear that guaranteed investment certificates are intended to be insured by this legislation provided their term is not more than the maturity mentioned by the minister, five years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION, MAKING OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
It would be my intention to recommend to the Governor in Council that guaranteed investment certificates of up to five years and debentures of loan companies up to five years would be covered.
February 14, 1967

Canada Deposit Insurance Corp.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION, MAKING OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to make only one further general comment on this clause. When the bill was at the second reading stage on February 3 I endeavoured to make my position very clear. I submitted that the minister had approached this problem in the wrong way. In my view the trouble is that parliament has abdicated its proper authority over banking. I am bothered because we have definitions such as the one in (j), "provincial institution", because there would be no such thing as a provincial institution in relation to deposit-taking if this parliament asserted its proper authority. Deposit-taking is the very heart and core of banking, and being the heart and core this parliament should assert its own exclusive authority over it. I am not going to argue further with the minister, but I wanted to make my position completely clear.
The minister ought to have moved to bring near banks under the supervision and control of this parliament, and having brought them under that supervision and control this legislation should have been universal and enforced in respect of all deposit-taking institutions. Because this has not been done I want to make it clear that I am not ready to be a party to the further abdication of the authority of this parliament. Because many of the clauses of this bill can be so interpreted, they will be passed so far as I am concerned on division.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION, MAKING OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
In this clause I believe we come up against the essence of the whole problem, and I fully subscribe to the views advanced by my colleague, the hon. member for Carleton, regarding the abdication of authority. Surely that suggestion has been supported by the minister as a result of his statement of a few minutes ago when he said it was all right for the government to recognize what are deposits in relation to federal institutions but it would be improper or impossible for the government to do so in relation to those institutions such as near banks operating under provincial charters of incorporation. That is the only right of supervision that should be granted to provincial authority in this field, the right of issuing a charter of incorporation.
The constitution makes it quite clear that the parliament of Canada has the exclusive right to deal with currency, interest and other financial matters. Let me refer to the precise terms of this exclusive right. In section 91 of

the B.N.A. Act the following are listed: subsection 14, currency and coinage; subsection 15, banking, incorporation of banks, and the issue of paper money; subsection 16, savings banks; subsection 18, bills of exchange and promissory notes; subsection 19, interest, and subsection 20, legal tender. What more could you require in this regard?
I find it incredible at this time that because of some unknown fear the federal government does not want to assume its exclusive right in the field of deposit insurance. Let me refer the minister to the representations of my colleague, the hon. member for Kamloops, at the committee hearings. Apparently there is a fear that because some isolated near bank might challenge the legislation such a challenge would ipso facto make this legislation suspect and non-operative. That proposition seems to be implicit in the minister's remarks. Quite contrary to the truth of the matter, there seems to be a feeling that if the parliament of Canada passed this bill and some corporation should challenge it it would not remain in effect. That is not so. It would remain in full effect until a judgment had been delivered ruling it ultra vires.
I want to know why we should allow the provinces to enter this field. I recognize the rights of provinces in their own spheres of jurisdiction, but this is one field which the constitution places exclusively within federal jurisdiction. Why should we now in respect of deposit insurance give the provinces the right to determine banking practice? The minister has said that the exact nature of deposits shall be determined by the interpretation of the provinces. Let me refer to the words of the minister as they appear at page 8 of the transcript of proceedings. He said that the Ontario minister, Mr. Rowntree, in his speech introducing the provincial legislation, had said that he was going to require all Ontario companies to join the federal scheme once it is in effect because he believes this problem can be handled more efficiently on a national than on a provinccial basis. I agree wholeheartedly with Mr. Rowntree in that respect.
What about the conflict in determining what is a deposit? What will happen to rights which may accrue to individuals during the interval between the provincial legislation and the federal scheme if a province determines a certain obligation in respect of a near bank and that determination is challenged by some of the holders? Where do we stand from
February 14, 1967

a federal point of view? Individuals and institutions are entitled to certainty. Some provincial governments may pass concurrent stopgap legislation. Why is it that the federal government will not recognize its responsibility in this regard?
If the minister is prepared to recommend to the Governor in Council that deposit obligations shall be covered for a period up to five years by deposit insurance, why does he not say so in the bill? The minister is making a decision by his statements to the house. Why does he not say so in the bill so that parliament will know what this corporation is going to do?
I may sound overly critical but I am concerned about the efficacy of this legislation. I am also concerned about the people who must be protected against delusion by the use of the phrase "guaranteed investment certificate" because the word "guarantee" only has a meaning in respect of an interest rate, not as to liquidity. If only these people knew that they could get just as good or better returns by going to reputable solicitors and placing their money in mortgages or by buying government of Canada securities they might not need so much protection, but we have to deal with all kinds of people. I suppose we must protect the most foolish of depositors.
Why, in legislation in respect of which we presumably have the initiative, are we unable to determine what is a deposit? After all, this bill is known as the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act. Perhaps I should paraphrase that and call it the Canada "we do not know" Insurance Act, because the government refuses to tell us what it means by a deposit. I fully agree with my colleague, the hon. member for Carleton, on this point. I am not going to labour the question of "provincial institution" under subclause (j). I shall have to reserve judgment on this matter, and the clause at best will have to pass, on division.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION, MAKING OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should just like to repeat what I said before, that there will be no uncertainty about the application of this legislation when the bylaws are issued. Full publicity will be given to the extent of the guarantee both to the institutions themselves and to the public. I can understand the comments of the hon. gentlemen who would like us now, before we have examined all these instruments, to define precisely what is a deposit. I regret that I am not in a position to do so, nor are my officials. They have a 23033-823
Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. fairly good idea of what should be included but they are very reluctant at this stage, before having examined the kind of instruments being issued by provincial institutions, to be too precise. I hope they will be able to do so shortly. They have been examining some of these instruments but have not completed their work.
May I comment upon another point. It is being assumed by the hon. member for Carleton and the hon. member for Edmonton West that one could define the business of banking as the business of taking deposits, but in fact, as we have seen from this discussion, what constitutes a deposit is subject to some uncertainty. I should like to draw attention to the Ontario act which was approved the other day, an act to establish the Ontario Deposit Insurance Corporation. That act says:
For the purposes of this act, a deposit shall be,
(a)	moneys deposited with a member institution in respect of which such institution is liable to the depositors;
(b)	moneys received under section 82 of the Loan and Trust Corporations Act by a trust company that is a member institution; and
(c)	debentures or like obligations issued by a loan corporation that is a member institution.

(a)	a deposit that is not payable in Canada or in Canadian currency;
(b)	so much of any one deposit, including interest thereon, as exceeds $20,000; and
(c)	so much of a deposit as is insured under the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act.

We would also exclude instruments made payable to bearer or instruments designed to be readily negotiable. Thus, for the future we would include demand deposits and term
February 14, 1967	COMMONS
deposits up to five years but to avoid confusion we would not include anything not specifically called a deposit on its face.
This might mean that the term "debenture" or "guaranteed investment certificate" would virtually disappear in respect of maturities of five years or less. Instead, such instruments might be called "deposit receipts" or some such term. However, if a company wanted to continue to issue debentures for periods of five years and under it could do so but the instrument would not be insured. If a company wanted to use the term "deposit" in respect of an instrument with a maturity over five years and not callable earlier, the instrument would have to be stamped "not insured".
For the transitional period we would propose that all obligations on a member institution's books at the date the act comes into force, in respect of moneys received prior to that date, would be insured no matter what they are called if they are, first, repayable on demand, second, repayable on notice of not more than five years, third, repayable on a fixed date not more than five years after the act comes into force. This would mean that some instruments called debentures and some called guaranteed investment certificates, issued prior to the date of the act, would be insured, but this would be justified on the ground that prior to that date there was no reason to use one name rather than another. For the transitional period, it would do no harm to extend the insurance a bit wider than people might expect.
That may illustrate the reason for our reluctance at this stage to define too precisely what a deposit is. Otherwise we would not have the flexibility it is so desirable to have in dealing with instruments that would normally be insured. If we define the instruments now in some limited way we may find we have interfered with some very desirable kind of deposit taking activity that we would wish to insure.

speechtext: I find it difficult to discover how a conflict of interest could arise. Perhaps the hon. gentleman would indicate the kind of circumstances in which there might be a conflict of interest, and on that basis I would be glad to comment.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION, MAKING OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
A case in which a conflict obviously arises is where the Superintendent of Insurance inspects and reports on a certain company. Then the private institution upon which he has reported, perhaps

Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. unfavourably, takes its case before the board of directors. The institution now finds it is dealing with the very person who made the unfavourable report, a person who is both the inquisitor and the judge. As 1 say, I have the highest of confidence in the integrity of the superintendent of insurance and of the inspector general of banks but a situation might easily occur in which great difficulty would ensue and I do not think such an invidious position should be allowed to arise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION, MAKING OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: May I point out to the hon. member that insurance cannot be withdrawn from a federal institution? Insurance can only be withdrawn from a provincial institution. It is compulsory for a federal institution.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION, MAKING OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Carle-ton has raised a point which escaped me entirely. I believe a difficulty arose in the United States during the last two years where the comptroller of the treasury has power to authorize the incorporation of banks. He gives them a certificate allowing them to commence business. There were two or three banks in the Pacific area which went bankrupt or got into difficulties to the extent that they closed their doors. They are, I believe subject to deposit insurance.
But let us look at the situation in Canada. A bank is authorized to commence business on the issuance of a certificate by the Treasury Board on the recommendation of the inspector general of banks. It is the inspector general of banks who gives the O.K. Cases might arise where an inspector general was over generous in his estimation of the ability of the incorporators of a bank to carry on the business of banking. Then the same inspector general sits in judgment as a member of the board of directors acting as a lender of last resort. One can see-and this is no reflection on the present incumbents of the two offices concerned-that the inspector general might be tempted to grant rather too generous terms in order to save his neck after he had authorized the issuance of a certificate to a banking institution when someone else might not have done so. He would be in a difficult position. It might be said that is only a theoretical possibility but unfortunately it is these theoretical possibilities which so often come to pass.
It seems to me on reflection that while the superintendent of insurance could carry out the duties of inspecting and reporting to the board the board must sit alone while assessing the reports made to it. The same applies
February 14, 1967

Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. to the inspector general of banks. I am persuaded that the view put forward by my hon. friend from Carleton is well founded and that notwithstanding the dignity of their offices and the probity of their reputations it is conceivable that the two officials who have been mentioned might be placed in a situation in which a conflict of interest could arise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION, MAKING OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
I find it difficult to agree with these arguments. I certainly think it would be a waste of public money if we had to duplicate the work which is being done by the inspector general of banks and the superintendent of insurance by having one federal official sitting in judgment on the other, which is in effect what is being suggested here. We created this corporation and provided that its directors should include the inspector general of banks and the superintendent of insurance because they were in the best position to know about the functioning of federal institutions; they have to inspect them in any event.
It seemed to us that the standards which they apply would be of the same kind in connection with insurance as were applied by them in connection with their responsibilities under other statutes. I find this is a highly theoretical and hypothetical argument and I suggest to the committee that if we were to start again to create a corporation we would appoint to its board of directors precisely those officers who are in the best position to judge the financial stability and the management standards of the corporations which they are supervising and which make applications for advances under the rediscount facilities. I can see little which would be gained by naming the deputy minister of trade and commerce or some other official rather than those officials who are most expert and who must report to the minister in any event about the operations of those institutions.

speechtext: I admit that the minister has an argument. It is an arguable case. So why would it be more invidious if they were to submit to the judgment of two others in a situation where there would be no conflict of interest?

speechtext: I am wondering whether there is not a conflict of interest in connection with clause 11, which I do not believe should occur. I am referring to subclauses (d) and (e). We have a peculiar situation here whereby a corporation that is a creditor of another corporation that is winding up becomes the liquidator and also the creditor corporation is capable of receiving, under subclause (e), the assets of the member institution from a liquidator or receiver thereof. I am just wondering whether this provision is not directly opposed to the Bankruptcy Act in that you have a creditor also acting as the liquidator. There may be a logical explanation for this but it seems to me incredible that the corporation should act in a dual capacity such as this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION, MAKING OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
This clause was designed to enable the corporation to wind up the affairs of a deposit-taking institution in the most orderly way possible and with the least loss to the corporation that is being wound up as well as the least loss to its depositors. The provision was designed deliberately for that reason. It may be unusual, but the circumstances under which one of these institutions would be wound up would be most unusual because the depositors would be insured.
It is certainly in the interests of the public at large that the assets of the insured institution should be disposed of in as orderly a fashion as possible. The corporation, we believe, would be in a better position sometimes to engage in the business of liquidating or receiving than anyone else of whom we can think. This does not mean that in every case the corporation would act as liquidator or receiver, but we believe it should be empowered to do so.

I should like to direct the attention of the committee to subclause 2, line 21, page 6. Under subclause 2 the directors of the corporation have all the powers conferred upon commissioners appointed under part II of the Inquiries Act. Then lines 21 and 22 of that clause read in part as follows:
-the directors may delegate such powers as occasion requires.
Here is a blanket delegation of authority under part II of the Inquiries Act. Part I of the Inquiries Act is of course the one that is more familiar because it gives power to royal commissions and the like. Part II deals with departmental investigations and is confined to a commissioner or commissioners appointed by a minister with authority of the governor in council. You know precisely who the commissioners are. The governor in council has to take responsibility for the person appointed as commissioner. These commissioners have substantial powers. They can compel the attendance of any person. They can compel such persons to produce documents and books. Where a person refuses to answer a question or produce any documents he is liable, on summary conviction, to a penalty of as much as $400. It seems to me that there is no real objection to this when the exercise is made by someone who is identifiable. But here we have a blanket delegation. We know not who may have the power under the Inquiries Act. Does the minister really believe that such a blanket delegation is necessary to carry out the purposes of this legislation? I

Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. think a considerable danger may creep in in this way.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, clause 13 of the bill seems to exempt certain depositors from insurance coverage. I believe one type of depositor has been omitted from this exemption. I have before me a financial statement of a Canadian bank which has just come to hand and I notice in this financial statement that there are several types of deposits listed. The liability for deposit is listed under five different nomenclatures, namely, government deposits, Canadian provincial government deposits, personal savings deposits, other deposits, and deposits by other banks.
I believe that in the categories "personal savings deposits" and "other deposits" there must be a number of deposits which are placed in a bank by trust companies and loan
(Mr. Bell (Carleton).]
companies which are incorporated under the federal Trust Companies Act or Loan Companies Act. There are also a number of deposits in this institution which are received from other banks. Initially those deposits from other banks and from trust and loan companies were insured under these acts. I submit that on that ground those deposits will in part, if clause 13 is left as it is, be covered a second time by deposit insurance, and I do not think that is the intention.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I propose to move an amendment to clause 13 which would exempt from insurance coverage deposits from any other federal institution as described in clause 9 of this bill, which clause defines federal institutions as banks and companies incorporated under the Trust Companies Act or the Loan Companies Act.
Specifically, the amendment I propose to suggest to clause 13 is as follows:
Delete "and" at the conclusion of subsection (b) and add a new subsection (c) as follows:
"a deposit of
(i)	a bank;
(ii)	a company incorporated by or pursuant to an act of the parliament of Canada that accepts deposits from the public and to which the Trust Companies Act or the Loan Companies Act applies; and
(iii)	a company the incorporation of which is continued by or pursuant to an act of the parliament of Canada that accepts deposits from the public and to which the Trust Companies Act or the Loan Companies Act applies.
Renumber the present subsection (c) as subsection (d).

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

In the first place I would point out that we are only insuring deposits up to $20,000. There are a great many people whose deposits will be insured but who will get very little insurance on the amount of their deposits. People with millions of dollars on deposit can get insurance only up to $20,000 of those millions. So even though we do in fact cover these deposits the amount of the coverage is quite infinitesimal.
Moreover, I think the question of double coverage can be answered in this way. Some institutions place deposits with other institutions. Indeed, one can imagine a situation where there is a complete circle. One institution deposits in another, the second in a third, the third in a fourth, the fourth in a fifth, and the fifth in the first. Only one of those institutions is likely to fall at one time. So the question of doubling up insurance is not a substantial point.
I would suggest to the committee that this introduces a quite unnecessary and unimportant amendment to the bill. It does nothing to make it more acceptable to the people and it certainly does not add anything to defray any cost to the institutions that might have to pay the small amount of insurance involved. But it would add enormously to the complications if it were to be accepted.

This is the clause which authorizes a province either to direct or to agree that an institution carrying on business in that province and incorporated within that province shall have the right to participate in this deposit insurance scheme. I have made many comments, both at the resolution stage and on second reading, about what I consider to be the unwarranted intrusion of the provincial authorities into the business of banking. They have no business whatsoever being there. At the moment they are being let in by default, and if this provision were challenged there would be justifiable argument that the provinces have no authority to engage in the business of banking or authorize the business of banking and near banking. I contend that they do not have the authority to direct near banks to participate in a federal system of deposit insurance.
I raised this point earlier with the minister, who did not answer it. Have the provincial governments the legislative authority either to direct or authorize provincially incorporated institutions, carrying on the business of near banking, to participate in a federal deposit insurance scheme? This point was discussed in the standing committee by Mr. Ryan, the department's legislation counsel, and my colleague, the hon. member for Kamloops, as recorded at page 24 of the unrevised transcript of the committee proceedings. Mr. Ryan was replying to a question and he said:
On which point, Mr. Chairman? On the authorization of the province? With respect to the authorization of the province of incorporation, I would like to point out a gray area that does exist ... These provincial institutions would be incorporated under the heading of a company with provincial objects. They would be authorized to carry out certain activities including the ones we are concerned about there, by their incorporating charter or their act, and they would also acquire in some cases all of their powers from that act, charter or statute, depending on the jurisdiction therein. In

some of these cases it may be beyond the powers of the company to take out insurance or to come into this scheme.
I do not know how it could be suggested by Mr. Ryan that this federal bill would cure a deficiency in the charter of a provineially incorporated company by providing that the provincial institution should be authorized by the province of its incorporation to apply for federal deposit insurance. I do not think any federal statute could do that.

In addition, I believe some trust companies are incorporated by private bills and a lot of cleaning up will be required in the provincial legislatures. Further, I question whether without legislative provision, without a special act authorizing a provincial cabinet or cabinet minister to direct provineially incorporated

Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. companies to participate in the federal scheme, provincial cabinets or ministers can so direct because the executive of a provincial government, like the executive council of the federal government, cannot act beyond the powers granted to it by some specific statute.
I doubt that there is any general provision whereby an order in council may be passed to do this. Some of the provincial authorities may say that simply because the premier of a province delivers a ukase that is sufficient, but I would like to know first whether the Minister of Finance is satisfied that provincial governments have the authority to direct provincially incorporated companies to participate in this scheme or to consent to their participation.
Second, since provineially incorporated companies are authorized to operate within the confines of a province, participation in the federal scheme would be an extraterritorial operation, and it may be that the charters of such companies are not wide enough to permit them to participate in any activity outside the province. In that case a provincial statute might be passed to cure defects in companies' charters. We agree with the principle that monetary policy and banking legislation are within the province of the federal parliament. We want to lump together all deposits by a particular person in a given institution, and this definition would not enable us to do that. This would treat each separate obligation as a deposit to be insured, and that is not our intention. We do not want anyone to circumvent the intention by getting insurance of more than $20,000 in any particular institution. This proposed definition would upset that intention.
We also need special provisions to deal with obligations on the books of institutions at the outset of the plan. speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext:
It is not my wish to carry on ad infinitum or ad nauseam or in any other way the discussion which the Minister of Finance and I were having last night. But I should like to say another word or two with respect to the point I was trying to make.
It is my contention that the Minister of Finance is trying to have it both ways with respect to the raising of taxes for old age pensions. On some occasions he tells us that the old age security fund must be kept in balance. He goes on to say that we must look ahead and consider the charges to be made on that fund in the years immediately in front of us, and that our whole plan of old age security pensions must be related to the concept of a fund which is kept in some kind of balance. But when I pointed out last night that less than half of the new taxes now being raised will go into the old age security fund he replied that what had to be taken into account was cash inflow and cash outflow, and not the fund. His exact words as recorded on page 12998 of Hansard for yesterday were:
The question of what goes into the fund and into general revenues is not relevant to the question of how much cash is needed.
In other words, the minister argued last night that although he is collecting $135 million in additional old age security taxes and putting that money into the old age security fund, what has to be considered is that the $155 million he is collecting from an increase in the sales tax, and which does not go into the fund, must be looked on as part of the inflow required to meet the outflow. In other words-and I see that I am stating the minister's position to his satisfaction, at any rate-the hon. gentleman is arguing that pensions are on a pay-as-you-go basis. This is what I have in mind when I say the Minister of Finance is trying to have it both ways. He throws the old age security fund at us when it suits his purpose. He would not agree to our contention that there was a balance in the fund at the present time and that no immediate increase is needed, asserting that one must look ahead and consider the needs of the future, when more money will have to be put into the fund. But when the minister is asked to explain the fact that he is not putting all the money into the fund, he says: "That is irrelevant; what matters is cash inflow and cash outflow." This is looking at the old age pension question strictly on a pay-as-you-go basis. Frankly, I favour that basis. Frankly, I think that was the essence of the

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext:
May I comment briefly, Mr. Chairman, on what has been said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. First of all, as he is aware and as I put on Hansard for December 19, page 11033, the fund itself during most of its life has been in substantial deficit. These deficits were to be found in the fund in every year from 1951-52 to 1959-60. There were small surpluses in 1960, 1961 and 1962. Then the fund went into deficit again. Part of these deficits were written off. This fund has never been, in that sense, in balance or anything like it.

In my speech on December 19, I dealt with two separate questions. The first question was the responsibility that parliament had toward the old age security fund, that is that it should be more or less kept in balance. This responsibility has been honoured more in the breach than in the observance. At any rate, that is the responsibility that is laid upon the government, to propose measures to keep the fund broadly in balance. As a means of doing that, I proposed that there should be an increase in the ceiling on the 4 per cent tax. This discharged the responsibility of the government toward the fund. Although as I say, in the past if you take the whole history of the fund there has never been enough in the fund to pay the costs of old age pensions, nevertheless as long as we have the fund we have a responsibility to keep it in balance.
I proposed changes in the old age security tax that will ensure that the fund is kept reasonably in balance for the foreseeable future. I did not feel I should make provision beyond a few years because that would be usurping the authority of later parliaments.
Then, as Minister of Finance, responsible for the finances of the country, I had to provide for the extra outlay over and above the amount that I was putting into the fund. From the point of view of the finances of the country, there was no place I could get the money except either from taxes or borrowing. There are no funds lying around in the old age security fund, for example, of which I am able to get hold. I did what I felt was wise, and what I think has appealed to the country as a whole, and that is that to the extent that government expenditures over all were being raised at that time by some $280 million, it was in the public interest that they should be offset by tax revenues, whether the moneys went into the old age security fund or whether they went into general revenues.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext: If there is no fund into which the minister can dip to find the money when we want to raise old age pensions, why does he argue that there is a fund that has to be replenished when, according to the books, it is in deficit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I have felt that I had a responsibility, since the old age security fund was established, of seeing it remains in balance or that it did not run into a big surplus, and I discharged that responsibility. Sometimes in the past it has been neglected. I did not feel, as Minister of Finance, that I should neglect that responsibility or
February 14, 1967

that duty. It was for this reason I made two separate provisions, one of them to keep the fund reasonably in balance in the foreseeable future, and the other to raise the remainder of the money which, one place or the other, I had to find.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext: I will keep my promise not to carry on this discussion interminably. It seems to me that the conversation we have had back and forth does underline the fact that this fund is just a device to be used in argument as to whether or not the pension should be increased. I hope that the day will come when the bookkeeping and the legislation will reflect the reality of our pension situation, namely that it is and should be on a pay-as-you-go basis.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext:
I listened with interest to the reply of the Minister of Finance concerning the necessity for this extra tax for old age pensions. He may feel that his approach has been well received across the country, but I can assure him he does have critics. Within the last few days, I have received this petition signed by over 90 people. I should like to read a bit of the preamble to the petition as an indication of the thoughts that are in the minds of some people concerning this matter:
We the undersigned members of the old age pensions group No. 17 Winfield, B.C. and sympathizers of this group do protest the insinuation of Finance Minister Sharp in his speech on television pertaining to the cost of the increase in old age pension; whereby like all skilful politicians who do not make an iron clad statement at any time, but imply that the cost of the increase in old age pensions is the cause for the increase in taxation and increase in taxation means increase in the cost of living.
The community from which this resolution comes is a very pleasant one indeed. It has a goodly proportion of old age security pensioners, so it was not a difficult task, I am sure, for people to obtain over 90 signatures to this petition. I can understand the minister when he says his approach was well received because I know from my own reading that he was given a very good press across this nation for what was regarded as a very hard-headed approach to this particular addition to payments that are generally regarded as being part of the welfare payments. In some ways this hard-headed approach, I suppose, provided a certain balance for the guaranteed annual income scheme of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, which in many quarters was regarded as being something rather radical. At the same time, these old age pensioners had this petition drafted to make a
Ways and Means
point. They go on to inquire why certain other expenses have not had certain taxes raised as a means of covering these expenditures. They mention the costs of Expo '67 and the cost of aid to foreign countries, for example. I am not using these examples to suggest in any way that these projects, Expo and aid to foreign countries, are not worthy. The point is that the Minister of Finance knows that they are very worthy. Indeed, he would not want to impose any tax on these particular sections of government spending because they would then provide too easy a target for criticism.
[DOT] (9:20 p,m.)
With the old age security pension, which everyone in the house agreed well over a year ago had to be increased, there was no alternative but to increase the pension. The minister is perfectly free to point out that a certain tax has been applied to produce the revenue required. Although this may annoy some sections of the populace, there can be absolutely no possible demand that any of the amount paid to the old age pensioners should be reduced to prevent this increase in tax. The minister is perfectly safe in designating a tax as providing for this particular area of government spending. I very much doubt whether within one year's time when the medicare plan comes into operation it will be spelled out very clearly to the people of Canada which particular section of the tax bill is applied toward offsetting the cost of that particular scheme.
The sad thing about the reference to a tax designated for this specific purpose is that it strikes again at the heart of the concept of the guaranteed annual income, a policy that I urged the minister to put into practice some time ago and which he took up.
I realize that the mini-budget is unnecessary. Had the government acted with dispatch the minister's main budget would have included the provision for the old age security pension increase. It was obvious at the time the budget was introduced that something had to be done; that the old age security pension was a national scandal which would have to be rectified some time during the year. There was no way around that. The thing is, I suppose, that there was a hope that the Canada Assistance Plan would prove sufficiently palatable to allow the postponing of any increase in the old age security pension.
When this proved unworkable, then the government was happy enough to bring in the

February 14, 1967
Ways and Means
guaranteed annual income scheme, because this was a difficult concept and required several months of working out, thus giving the Minister of Finance time to dream up additional sources of extra revenue. But this hits at the heart of the idea that was in the mind of the minister of health and welfare when he talked of guaranteeing a certain income. It is basic to the idea of the guaranteed income that it is given as a right of the people.
The unfortunate thing about using this tax increase in this way is that the supplement to the old age income takes on the appearance of an extravagance instead of a right. It is as if the minister were saying: "All right, if you want that you will pay for it another way". I am sure that this is causing a great deal of annoyance, even anguish, to our old age security pensioners, many of whom regret that the basic pension was not first raised and the guaranteed income used to supplement that amount. Some of these pensioners will not profit very much from this supplement.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think these petitioners are on good ground. The last paragraph is as follows:
Our government talks strongly of the wealth and prosperity of our people. We think finance minister Sharp should apologize to the old age pensioners for such an insinuation. If the government needs a scapegoat why don't they get someone more able to fight back than the old age pensioners?
Certainly this group, Mr. Chairman, is not in a position to fight very effectively against this measure that will, after all, provide them with some assistance. However, I regret that the minister, perhaps through lack of foresight or through failure to realize the determination of the people of Canada to insist that something be done for our old age security recipients, should have chosen this particular area to teach his hard-headed lesson in economics to the people of this country.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to hold up the committee but I should like to reiterate my previous comment that this tax is hitting the very people to whom the minister in his budget speech on December 19 intimated he was attempting to present a Christmas present. This increase in the sales tax on all goods other than building materials, and so forth, of 1 per cent is going to hit the very people it presumably is intended to help.
As I have tried to argue before, I am not in a position to say what a difference of 1 per cent actually means to the consumers, but at any rate it does amount to a substantial sum to the pensioners who will have to buy clothes and other essentials out of their $75 plus. I say "plus" because a means test is applied above that amount, and in most cases the old age security recipients will not get the full amount.
This tax will undoubtedly increase the cost of living. We know that the people of Canada as a whole are being taxed to the very limit and beyond. We are now imposing a 1 per cent increase in the sales tax and this will affect everyone. I am not pleading the case of the medium income or high income groups; I am pleading the case of the low income group, people who will definitely be affected by this increase to the same degree as people in the higher income brackets.
I can only repeat that this increase in sales tax is detrimental to the welfare of the country. It will certainly increase the cost of living and will hit those old age security recipients whom the minister has intimated were going to be given a Christmas present.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while we had some discussion on the other resolution we did not register any objection to it. We are in favour of the idea of raising the ceiling of the other tax; as a matter of fact we think it should be taken off altogether. But this resolution is a different kettle of fish. We are opposed to this increase and we shall make this clear at the appropriate opportunity if we do not manage to make it clear in debate.
We think that a further increase in sales tax at this time is inimical to the functioning of our economy. We think it is unfair to the consumers of this country, and that means all of the people of Canada. We think it is particularly unfair to the old age pensioners, on two counts. In the first place it is unfair to them because it effects an immediate increase in the cost of many items they have to buy,
February 14, 1967

and therefore cuts into the increased pension that some of them will be able to get.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
It is also unfair to our old age pensioners, and this is the second point I alluded to a moment ago, because it creates across Canada the notion that this tax is made necessary because of the increase in the pension. No matter how much the minister may want to argue the difference between cash balances and fund balances, this legislation is drafted to make clear that the 1 per cent increase now being asked for in the sales tax is not for old age security purposes.
At present the federal sales tax is 11 per cent, made up of 8 per cent as a general tax and 3 per cent for old age security. If this resolution and the bill to be based on it passes, we shall have a 12 per cent federal sales tax, of which 9 per cent will be general tax and 3 per cent will still be for old age security purposes. In other words, when people have to pay 12 per cent instead of 11 per cent they are contributing the additional 1 per cent in sales tax to the general revenues of this country, despite the impression left across Canada that this additional percentage point is related directly to the old age pension question.
These two quantities, $290 million of taxation against $280 million of increased pension make, I would say, 99 people out of 100 think that what I have alluded to is the purpose for this increase in the sales tax. In this connection there is no more reason why old age pensioners should be labelled as responsible for a particular segment of our taxation than other items on which we spend federal money. If we are to follow this principle, why not have our taxes divided into little compartments, so that we know how much we pay for national defence, airports, to subsidize the railways, customs services and a whole raft of things. The hon. member for Edmonton West says it might have been further divided-by provinces.
We do not do that. We accept the theory of government finance and the theory of civilization as we know it, that taxes levied according to ability to pay are put into a common fund. Out of that fund we meet the costs of the services required for our kind of society. I do not think old age pensioners should be singled out for the complaint that is levelled against them by this kind of taxation method, that they are a particular charge on the funds of the country.
Ways and Means
Even calling these things transfer payments is not really in keeping with the kind of society we have today. I want to register most strongly our objection to this tax, to this increase from 11 per cent to 12 per cent, to this increase in general sales tax from 8 per cent to 9 per cent. I want also to register my strong objection to the way this has been done, creating the impression that old age security is this kind of particular charge on the revenues of this country, on our economy. Old age security has as much right as a charge on our total revenues as has national defence, roads, airports and any of the other services we provide. That is the way it should be, instead of this business of pinning it down and somehow attaching a stigma to our old age pensioners.
Let it be clear, if we can possibly make it clear to the country, that the sales tax change being asked for is not for an increase in the old age part of the sales tax. It is for an increase in general sales tax. When the tax becomes 12 per cent, if it goes through, the old age security tax will still be 3 per cent. The general sales tax is being raised to 9 per cent, and when people have to pay this extra money it will go into the general funds of this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, many of the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre are applicable to the criticism of the division of tax. The minister tried to justify the imposition of this tax at the time of the budget. He justified it as paying for increases in the old age security. The position of this party was that there was sufficient in the old age security fund to pay for the increases which, after all, will not be disbursed until late next month or possibly in April. There was no great rush to get money into the old age security fund.
But when we look at the tax increase, that is not the way it will be done. None of this money will go into the old age security fund. It will go into the consolidated revenue fund. Next year, if the old age security fund has enough in it to pay the demand upon it, the minister can apparently turn around and use any of this money in the consolidated revenue fund for practically any purpose. One wonders at all this when he looks at the minister's position with regard to the necessity for delivering his budget late in December, after many postponements. As I said in the budget debate, the minister's dilemma was whether to tax or not to tax.

February 14, 1967
Ways and Means
He had to justify giving the budget speech. In August or September he had unfortunately said, apparently to take pressure off the government because of the increase in the cost of living, that he would bring down a budget. That pressure was the primer of the movement. Of course, the budget must be justified by some tax measure.
How convenient it was, Mr. Chairman,- how convenient. There is the promise to provide up to $30 a month for persons under a so-called income test. There was no need for money until March. We must remember that the tax was not to spoil Christmas, because the voters might get excited; so, from January 1 we had a 1 per cent increase in the sales tax.
The government came along and said to the older people of this country: "Look at the good boys we are. We are giving you a fine Christmas present, a fine end-of-the-year present with the increase in old age security payments for those people who need them." I should not say, "need them", I should say, "for those whose incomes are below a certain level."
