But they did not turn around and say to them "We will take all of that increase, plus some more, from each and every one of you." There is no doubt that the full sales tax is paid, whether it be by a four-year-old infant who buys a taxable item, or an 85 year old senior citizen. The tax is paid by all concerned, and therefore the older persons are paying their share of the increase through taxation.
It was the same thing two years ago at the time of the introduction of the Canada Pension Plan. There was a gap for persons aged 65 to 70 and the government came along with a great fanfare of trumpets, introducing an amendment, something like a little trailer or rumble seat operation, whereby over a period of five years the government would pay old age security to older people progressively downwards from age 70 to 65. But the government did not tell those people that they were going to lose their $500 exemption under the Income Tax Act, and there was that loss for people between the ages of 65 and 70. There was also to be a diminution in benefits under the War Veterans Allowance Act.
Oh yes, Mr. Chairman, the government was handing it out with one hand, and with a number of hands was withdrawing a good deal of the benefit that elderly persons were deriving from the increase in old age security.

I believe the government should admit what it is doing, should tell old age pensioners just how their pension increase is being financed and how much they themselves will have to pay for it; but I will wager my bottom dollar that there will not be one piece of government propaganda to that effect when they describe social welfare measures. Millions of dollars were spent to publicize the Canada Pension Plan, but the publicity never mentioned the negative aspects of the amendments to the Old Age Security Act, the Income Tax Act, and the War Veterans Allowance Act to indicate what was being withdrawn from the elderly people.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare goes around the country trumpeting about this increase to $105, this so-called guaranteed minimum income for elderly persons, but he does not dare tell them that they are paying for part of it through this increase in tax.
This is the only justification for the minibudget because in the minister's speech, which no doubt somebody prepared for him, we heard a lot of self-evident observations and platitudes with regard to the state of the economy. It was interesting to note that many of the members on the government side did not even utilize the time available to them during the budget debate to review the economy or to plead with respect to particular problems presented to them by their constituents. A budget debate is much like a Throne Speech debate. Participation by members on the government side is expected to be equal to that on the opposition side, or even greater if the government has a majority. This is as it should be if there is going to be meaningful examination of the state of the economy.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to speak briefly on the amendments to the Excise Tax Act which raised the sales tax from 8 per cent to 9 per cent on most of the articles sold in Canada. Like other hon. members I deprecate the attitude of the government in blaming old age pensioners for this increase in the sales tax. The government has to get the money somewhere, but it turns around and says, "You dear old people over 70 years of age are the cause of all this." To my mind that is wrong. As other speakers have pointed out, it was wrong in inception, wrong from the start, and wrong at the finish.
Members sitting on the government benches have never changed their minds with regard 23033-8261
Ways and Means
to old age pensioners. In 1957 those members were only too glad to say, "We are going to give you $6." From that time on they were known as the Six Buck Boys. On that occasion everybody in opposition said, "No, that is not enough." The Liberal party lost the ensuing election.
When the Conservative party took office it said the minimum rise should be $15, and that is what we paid. Later it gave a further increase over and above that $15. The old age pension was $40 under the Liberal regime. It was increased to $55 under the Conservatives and again to $65 under the Conservatives. Then what happened?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext: It went up to $105.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance

speechtext:
The minister says it is up to $105. Never has a more stupid statement been made in this house. If you will bear with me for a minute, Mr. Minister, I will tell you exactly why I say that. You were one of the people who sat in this house after the 1963 election, during which you promised the old age pensioners $75, and said, "No, no, no; we never said $75. That was only an election promise and we really did not mean it."
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
Many said that they did not even promise it. I listened to this on many, many platforms. I heard Liberal candidates stand up and say "$75-the heck with that; $100 it should be". In any event, what I am trying to tell the minister and all his colleagues is that after coming back here, for years after 1963 they resisted any increase in the pension from $65.
I might point out that the Conservative government, on supply, brought in a motion to the effect that it should be raised immediately to $75. The Liberal government, sitting over there in minority, suddenly realized that everybody on this side on the house, the Conservatives, the New Democratic Party, the Social Credit party and the Creditiste party, were saying that this must be put through. At that stage, mealy mouthed, they finally came through and brought it in. They now say, as the minister said, "We are giving $105". They are not giving that. They are saying that it must be proven by a means test that it is needed. So, do not say that you are giving $105, Mr. Minister, because you are not giving it to all old age pensioners.
In rising tonight I did not intend to prolong this question. It was only the rather silly interjection by the Minister of Finance which

February 14, 1967
Ways and Means
prompted me to continue with this. Today Canada is fighting for export markets. The sales tax is one thing which cuts in so deeply into our ability to enter into export trade. It not only affects our ability to produce in our own country for the export market, but also helps those who wish to sell to Canada from other countries. This 11 per cent sales tax on production equipment and building materials is bad enough. It cuts tremendously into Canada's ability to cope with outside manufacturers, those who would export into Canada. There is no question in my mind that the rather stupid raising of the sales tax will produce another inequity; that is, Canada's ability to stop those who would bring into Canada goods, and our ability to export outside. We fought this all through the years. When the former minister of finance brought this in I rather believe it was hoped by many members of the Liberal party that it would be discarded as another example of silliness on the part of the minister. Apparently, however, it is being perpetuated; not only that, it is being increased now from 11 per cent to 12 per cent.
Let me reiterate one more point. To step up and blame our old age pensioners for this, to my mind is completely and utterly wrong. Once again may I close by saying to the Minister of Finance that to say to the old age pensioners they will receive $105 is an utterly ridiculous statement. This is a statement which the minister has interjected from time to time as other hon. members were speaking.
It is great propaganda to say that the old age pensioners will get $105 a month, an extra $30. This just is not so. Many old age pensioners in Canada will not be entitled to qualify for this additional $30. As I have said, this was a stupid statement for the minister to make. There is no argument which he can put forward which will suggest otherwise.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should not like to gloss over the 1 per cent tax increase. Naturally, the hon. minister can say: We are increasing the sales tax by 1 per cent to help the aged who would have no other source of income. But on closer look, we see that this 1 per cent increase leads to inflation, in fact it leads to an increase of far more than 1 per cent, it increases the cost of living by almost 4 per cent.

And in order to prove my contention, Mr. Chairman, let me illustrate my point by referring to an article or object a manufacturer would sell for $10.
The federal sales tax is said to have been increased from 8 to 9 per cent but, in fact, in view of the other 3 per cent federal sales tax, the hidden federal sales tax will rise from 11 to 12 per cent.
Let us take the case of an article a manufacturer sells for $10. Formerly, with the federal sales tax of 11 per cent, the article was sold by the manufacturer for $10 plus $1.10, that is the 11 per cent tax, which totalled $11.10. Since the sales tax has now reached 12 per cent, the wholesaler will have to pay $11.20 for the same $10 article. If the wholesaler wants to make his usual 10 per cent profit, since the article which used to cost him $11.10 and which he sold for $12.20 will now cost him $11.20, he will have to sell it for $12.32. This shows that the price of an article increases by more than 1 per cent when it passes from the manufacturer to the wholesaler.
If the commercial traveller also wants to make his profit of, say, 10 per cent, he will not make it on the $12.20 he used to pay, but on the price he must pay today, which is $12.32. This means that the retailer will pay not $13.42, but $13.55 because of this 1 per cent increase. And the retailer, who still makes a profit of 10 per cent on that, will sell it for $14.70, or if he sold it before for $14.76, he will sell it today for $14.91. This means that, in the past, the federal government could get 10 cents on $10 and that today the retailer sells it for 15 cents more. And when the retailer charges the 6 per cent provincial tax, he does charge it also on that federal tax. In the past, he charged 6 per cent on the 11 per cent federal tax; today, the federal government will charge the sales tax on 12 per cent, which means that, with the provincial tax, the $10 price will reach $15.81 instead of $15.64, and the price will be 17 cents higher. And the federal government will only get 10 cents out of that. But, through the process, the profit margins remaining the same, the consumer will pay 17 cents more, even if the federal government gets only 10 cents, which means that the cost of living has practically gone up 2 points.
And when the cost of living increases by two points, the worker asks for a salary increase of two points, that is, 2 per cent. This will not increase his purchasing power at all, but will merely counter-balance the higher
February 14, 1967

cost of living. We have now reached a 4 point increase in the cost of living, that is, goods will cost 40 cents more, whereas the federal government will only have obtained 10 cents, the elderly will only have received a 10 cent increase and the purchaser, the payer, the consumer will pay 40 cents more for any $10 item.
Well, Mr. Chairman, the minister wants to collect an additional 1 per cent tax in order to increase the old age pensions of those with an income less than $105 per month, but let us keep in mind, on the other hand, that the consumer will be paying 4 per cent more, rather than 1 per cent, in sales tax, but-

As a result of their comments to individuals who have not had such an opportunity it has been suggested that this train should make a repeat tour next year in order that as many Canadians as possible may have
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion the opportunity of seeing this train before it is dismantled.
I should like to read one letter, Mr. Speaker, to illustrate the type of letter I have received in his connection:
Dear Mr. Herridge:
I am writing as a temporary resident of Vancouver and a permanent resident of Kootenay West (Rossland); also because you have a reputation for answering all your mail.
I see that the minister has noted that fact. The letter continues:
The centennial train has just left Vancouver after a very successful visit-people wanting to visit the train had to wait in line for up to four hours throughout the time it was here. Several times radio announcers warned people to stay home because they didn't have a chance of getting on the train. This is my question: What is going to happen to the train after centennial year? Is there any chance that it will be able to make a repeat tour next year-including the places to be missed this year? I hope the answers are affirmative. Incidentally, I was one of the many who did not see the train and would very much like to see it. We were turned away because of the crowds.
Yours sincerely,
Mrs. G. C. Bilodeau.

HISTORIC SITES AND MONUMENTS-RESTORATION OF HOME OF SIR ALEXANDER GALT
speechtext:
My question was addressed to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in his capacity as minister responsible for the Historic Sites and Monuments Board. It was intended to lead to positive action; it was not an attempt to cry over spilled milk.
I feel it is useless at this time to try to find out who was to blame for the demolition of what we call Galt House, though I do believe the minister should make a complete and detailed study of this matter, and that those responsible should be punished.
Sir Alexander Galt emigrated to Sherbrooke in 1835 and in 1849 was elected from Sherbrooke to the legislative assembly of Canada, where he served until 1867. He sat in the House of Commons until 1872. He was a delegate to the Charlottetown and Quebec conferences of 1864 and to the Westminster

DEBATES	February 14. 1967
conference of 1866 and was one of the chief architects of the British North America Act. In 1867 he became the first finance minister of the Dominion and in 1880 was appointed the first Canadian high commissioner in London.
Time does not permit me to continue with this great man's accomplishments, but I wanted to draw these facts to the attention of the house to show why we felt it was so important to preserve his home. I understand the minister has announced that a monument, not just a plaque but a real monument, will be placed in Sherbrooke to commemorate this statesman. Of course we appreciate this very much. Nevertheless the Eastern Townships Historical Society has requested that the remaining portion of what we now call Galt House, the stable, or the carriage house-the portion of the house which was attached to the original house and which formed part of it-be preserved. Fortunately this portion was not demolished when the original home was destroyed. The preservation of the carriage house would, we feel, be preferable to the erection of a monument which in itself would have little of historical value. I may say that I have quoted a portion of an editorial which appeared in one of the local newspapers.
I do not wish to labour this question, I should like the minister to give us, if he can, a definite date on which he and the officials of the historic sites division can come to Sherbrooke to study this matter. At the same time I would be glad of an assurance that his visit will be made before any definite decision is reached with regard to the carriage house. We understand that the minister is burdened with other work in the department, but I should like to suggest to the hon. gentleman that he take the opportunity of meeting the people in the area and hearing them explain the historical value which they attach to this site-that he should visit the area before a final decision is taken and discuss with those people who are interested exactly what his department is prepared to do.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Indian Affairs and Norihern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: HISTORIC SITES AND MONUMENTS-RESTORATION OF HOME OF SIR ALEXANDER GALT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems the happiest circumstance surrounding the commemoration of Sir Alexander Galt is the interest of the Eastern Quebec Historical Society. This is one of the finer evidences, I think, of the value of perpetuating places of history in this nation. We are apologetic still, and very sorry, over the disaster which befell our efforts to move the
February 14. 1987	COMMONS
house itself. It was going to be demolished in any case. We hurriedly put in a contractor who told us he thought he could move it, but when he touched the house it fell apart. We do not want the same thing to happen in any attempt to move what the hon. member calls a carriage house, but which I believe was actually a stable. We think that probably the same thing would happen in that case, because it is set upon rock. When we move the rock of 100 years ago, it just falls apart and we do not want that to happen again.
What we are planning at the present time, and the Historic Sites and Monuments Board has reviewed this on a number of occasions now, is to use a plot of land at the side of the estate about 300 feet from where the house stood and erect there a monument to Sir Alexander Galt. We have commissioned the well known sculptor Madame Guite of Quebec to make submissions to us which will be studied by the Historic Sites and Monuments Board. I want to assure my hon. friend that the officers of the historic sites division are going to the site later this month and will review the whole situation again.
We came to the opinion, based upon the recommendation of the Historic Sites and Monuments Board, that commemoration at this site was extremely important to Canadians. We intend to make a commemoration there worthy of Canada and worthy of Sir Alexander Galt and his contributions to Canada. I would be very happy indeed, and I will assure the hon. member that some time this year I will endeavour, to visit the site myself. We will seek there the co-operation, which I know will be forthcoming, of the historical society, because of all the efforts made theirs is the most valuable to the area and to his memory.

EDUCATION-REQUEST FOR INCREASED ASSISTANCE TO CANADIAN STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am just looking for the representatives of the Prime Minister's office and of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The subject matter which I wish to discuss tonight is, I believe, very important since it relates to Canadian university students. Evidently no one in the Prime Minister's office or the office of the Secretary of State for External Affairs is interested. I understood that on this late show there was to be at least some representative of a minister Who would supply some information on this subject. However, in view of the information I obtained in answer to
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion question No. 2090 on the order paper, I feel the Canadian university students will answer for themselves. Then, perhaps the Prime Minister or the Secretary of State for External Affairs will give a more attentive ear than they are giving tonight.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to our external aid program under which students from foreign countries are helped to attend Canadian universities. I was astonished to learn from the Secretary of State for External Affairs that the average amount of money Canada extends to these students is $5,467.29 per annum per student.
How many Canadian students get that kind of money to go to school? Our students have to do part time work in restaurants to pay their way through school, because their parents cannot afford to finance the entire cost.
o (10:20 p.m.)
I have been wondering why there has been so much bickering and hollering over foreign aid. Canadian students at the present time are undergoing an injustice. We finance foreign students to come to Canada to study, students who do not have the same problems Canadian students have. As far as finances are concerned, they are treated better than Canadian students.
I would ask how many Canadian students have about $5,500 a year to go through university? This amounts to $22,000 over a four-year term; and this is the average figure, Mr. Speaker. Out of 900 odd students only 515 graduated. Some of these might have required $6,000; the average was $5,500. These are students who have been changing cars every year. They are about the brightest students from these underdeveloped countries. Some of them do not have to work so hard and some attend a minimum of courses. Their financial problems are minimal compared with some Canadian students who have to slave their way through university.
I am not saying that this amount is too much, but not many Canadian students can afford to pay this sum. If we can spend this amount on foreign students, then we can spend the same amount on Canadian students. The federal government is going to award 10,000 grants to Canadian students. Yet it can afford external aid to the tune of $259,360,000 in 1965, which is a staggering figure.
I believe the purpose of external aid is missed entirely. In one way or another the goals and aims of the external aid program are unrealistic. We give these foreign students
13062	COMMONS DEBATES	February 14, 1967
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion an education or train them at a Canadian university for a trade or for the professional field, so they can return to their homeland to render their country a service. The problem is, Mr. Speaker, they do not go back home. Some of the responsibility for this is upon the federal government at the present time for providing them with a high standard of living. No wonder they do not go back home to an underdeveloped country, when we spend $22,000 on them over four years.
The United Nations has also produced some staggering figures in this regard. Some 85,000 medical doctors did not return to India after taking their course. They are scattered around the world. They might not all be in Canada, but anyone versed in external affairs knows that Canada's reputation internationally is such that if they are trained here they are fitted to enter any country they desire. I know of no restrictions. At present we are not doing India a service in this respect, or any of the other underdeveloped countries; we are doing them a disservice. We are taking their best students away from them. They do not return to their homeland to practise what they have learned here, which was the main objective of the external aid program.
I suggest this program should be revised as soon as possible. Our own Canadian students are in no way assisted by these circumstances at the present time. They have to attend the same universities and undergo the same expenses as foreign students. Very seldom can they raise more than $2,000, but they have to compete with students from other countries who are financed by the Canadian government through Canadian taxpayers. It is the government's responsibility to look into the question of paying this $5,500 to Canadian students.
